hints.S25_A1: It took THREE YEARS, so this is slow designing, building and improving - not a single click. Ask: which word means to create something new over a long time? 'Download' takes seconds; 'destroy' and 'discard' get rid of things.
hints.S25_A2: The dash explains it: every tiny REFLECTION is perfectly clear, and the screen is compared to a MIRROR. Ask: which adjective describes a flat, even surface with no bumps? 'Heavy' and 'small' say nothing about a surface.
hints.S25_A3: TURNING SEAWATER INTO DRINKING WATER takes a series of steps, one after another. Ask: which word names a method built from ordered steps? An 'excuse' or a 'hobby' could never help millions of people.
hints.S25_A4: NOBODY EXPECTED news this exciting, and the invention can CHARGE A PHONE IN THIRTY SECONDS. Ask: does the idiom describe delight, illness, or danger? 'Under the weather' means ill; 'in hot water' means in trouble.
hints.S25_A5: To MAKE IT SIMPLER, the COMPLICATED feature has to go. Ask: which phrasal verb means to remove something from a design? 'Bring in' would add it back, and 'hold up' would only delay the LAUNCH.
hints.S25_B1: The subject is EVERYONE, not 'the engineering team'. Words like everyone and nobody act like ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s?
hints.S25_B2: HAVE is already there, so the blank must be the form that partners with it. Ask: after 'have', do we use the plain verb, the -ing form, or the past participle? This verb is regular, so it simply takes -ed.
hints.S25_B3: The battery RAN OUT - a sudden event breaking into an activity already under way. Ask: which form shows an action still in progress in the past? A plain past verb reports only a finished action.
hints.S25_B4: THAN compares this laptop with LAST YEAR'S VERSION - exactly two models - and the adjective is a long one. Ask: do long adjectives take -er, or do they need a comparing word in front? 'Powerfuller' is not English; 'most' is for three or above.
hints.S25_B5: DATA is one uncountable mass: you never say 'one data, two datas'. Ask: which quantity word measures an amount rather than counting separate items? 'Many', 'few' and 'a few' all count things one by one.
hints.S25_B6: The statement is positive, and its verb CHANGED is a past simple verb - there is no 'to be' verb anywhere in it. Ask: after a positive statement, is the tag positive or negative? And which helper stands in for a past simple verb?
hints.S25_B7: BY ALEXANDER GRAHAM BELL shows the telephone received the action - it could hardly build itself. Ask: which choice is passive, and does it match a year long finished? A passive verb needs a helper plus a past participle.
hints.S25_B8: TOLD + somebody + an instruction. Ask: after 'told its programmers', does English use the plain verb, the -ing form, or the infinitive with 'to'? Reported orders always follow the one same pattern.
hints.S25_C1: Edison was ALREADY A FAMOUS INVENTOR, so the light bulb did not make him famous - this is not a reason. Ask: which joining word marks the POINT IN TIME at which he SWITCHED it on?
hints.S25_C2: Why CANDLES? The second half tells you: they had NO OTHER WAY of seeing after dark. Ask: which joining word introduces the reason for something? 'So' would give a result instead - the wrong direction.
hints.S25_C3: Three places are being listed: HOMES, SCHOOLS, OFFICES. Every one of them has electric lamps; nobody is choosing between them. Ask: which joining word ADDS the last item of a list? 'Or' would offer a choice.
hints.S25_C4: One machine filled A WHOLE ROOM; the other fits in a POCKET. The two halves clash. Ask: which joining word signals a contrast, a surprise, a sharp difference? 'And' would simply add a second fact of the same kind.
hints.S25_C5: The machines BROKE DOWN first; the ENGINEERS WORKED LONG HOURS as a consequence. Ask: which joining word introduces the RESULT of a problem? 'Because' would flip the order, making the engineers the cause.
hints.S25_C6: Two activities run side by side from start to finish: you LISTEN TO MUSIC for the whole time that you JOG. Ask: which joining word means 'at the same time as', across a stretch of time rather than one instant?
hints.S25_C7: The sentence admits a good thing (lives MUCH EASIER), then turns against it (NEW PROBLEMS, TOO MUCH SCREEN TIME). Ask: which joining word opens a sentence to say 'despite this fact'? 'Because' would make the problems a reason.
hints.S25_C8: EITHER is the giveaway: it always needs a partner, offering one of two choices - a SELF-DRIVING CAR, a FLYING TAXI. Ask: which joining word presents alternatives? 'And' would mean both arrive together.
hints.S25_D1: The dash explains the blank: DOING MORE WORK IN LESS TIME with LESS EFFORT. It follows 'more', so it must describe the DEVICE. Ask: which box word means getting a job done without waste? 'Gadget' names a thing, not a quality.
hints.S25_D2: The sentence defines the blank for you: any SMALL ELECTRONIC DEVICE, from a SMARTWATCH to a POCKET CALCULATOR. It follows 'A', so it names a thing. Ask: which box word is that thing? A 'circuit' is only a part inside it.
hints.S25_D3: The clue comes straight after the blank: inventions that SOLVE PROBLEMS IN COMPLETELY NEW WAYS. Ask: which box word describes something new, original and creative? 'Obsolete' means out of date - the exact opposite.
hints.S25_D4: Inventors REGISTER it in order to PROTECT THEIR IDEA BY LAW. Ask: which box word names an official document granting legal rights? A 'circuit' or a 'gadget' is hardware, never paperwork.
hints.S25_D5: The dash spells it out: SENDING DATA THROUGH THE AIR without any CABLES. Ask: which box word describes technology that needs no cable at all? 'Manual' means done by hand and has nothing to do with cables.
hints.S25_E1: The underlined word is a plural, but the -ES ending has been over-applied. Ask: which nouns truly take -ES? Only the hissing endings: bus/buses, box/boxes, watch/watches, brush/brushes. Does this word end in any of those?
hints.S25_E2: The favourite exhibit belongs to the two GUIDES; the sentence is not pointing at a place. Ask: does the underlined spelling mean 'over at that spot', or 'belonging to them'? They sound alike but are spelt differently.
hints.S25_E3: TWO of them, so a plural is needed - and this noun refuses a simple -s. Ask: how does the word MAN change in the plural? It swaps a vowel, exactly as woman and child change shape rather than take an ending.
hints.S25_E4: Find the subject: the INTERACTIVE DISPLAYS - then count them. Ask: is that one thing, or many? A long subject can trick you, so match the verb to the head noun, never to the word closest to the blank.
hints.S25_E5: The NAMES belong to the inventors - many owners, not one. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only make a plural? When the owners are many, does the apostrophe go before the -s, or after it?
hints.S25_F1: The second sentence names THE TELEPHONE all over again. Ask: where must the relative pronoun sit - straight after the noun it stands for? And what must you delete from the second sentence so that the subject is not repeated twice?
hints.S25_F2: A yes/no question turned into REPORTED speech. Ask: which small joining word follows ASKED? Does the question keep its inverted order, or turn into a normal statement? And what happens to 'you' and to 'can'?
